seo.title: ClickHouse client for {devices}
seo.description: Query ClickHouse over HTTP or HTTPS, read Plan, Pipeline and Estimate EXPLAIN output, manage MergeTree parts and partitions, and watch mutations.

header.title: ClickHouse client for {devices}
header.lead: Run analytical SQL over ClickHouse’s HTTP interface, read a query’s plan, pipeline or row estimate, and manage MergeTree parts and partitions from the table’s Parts tab. Long queries report rows read as they run, and Stop ends them on the server.

sections.title: Connect
paragraphs: Give the host and the HTTP port, a user and, if you like, a database. Changing database happens in place, and an open tab stays on the database it started on. <ui>View > Sidebar as Tree</ui> shows the server’s databases as a tree you expand in place.

Choose any SSL mode to switch to HTTPS. A port of 443 or 8443, the one ClickHouse Cloud uses, turns on Verify Identity, which checks the certificate against your CA file or the system trust store. Verify CA needs a CA file, and a client certificate and key reach servers that require mutual TLS.
Without TLS, reach a remote server through an <network>SSH tunnel</network> rather than sending plain HTTP across the network.

sections.title: Query and edit
paragraphs: Each query carries its own id and asks for progress, so a long one reports rows read as it goes. Stop sends KILL QUERY for that id, and the connection’s query timeout reaches the server.

The <explain>Explain menu</explain> offers Plan, Pipeline, AST, Syntax and Estimate. The indented output is drawn as a diagram or a tree, and Estimate shows the rows, marks and parts a query would read.

Grid edits go out as INSERT, ALTER TABLE … UPDATE and ALTER TABLE … DELETE, with Preview SQL first. ClickHouse runs updates and deletes as background mutations, so a save means accepted, not yet applied; system.mutations shows the progress. A materialized view opens read-only.
A result holding ClickHouse point or ring tuples opens on the Map view. A query with its own FORMAT clause shows the server’s raw output in one column, so leave the clause off to get a grid.

sections.title: Tables, parts and partitions
paragraphs: A table opens with Structure, Indexes, DDL and Parts tabs. Indexes shows the sorting key and the data-skipping indices, and DDL shows the full CREATE TABLE, engine and settings included.
Parts lists every part from system.parts with its partition, rows, size on disk, modification time and active flag, and runs Optimize, Drop Partition and Detach Partition from there.

The Structure tab adds, modifies and drops columns and drops data-skipping indices. The sorting key and primary key are fixed when a table is created, so add a data-skipping index with ALTER TABLE … ADD INDEX, and recreate the table for other changes.

sections.title: Monitor
paragraphs: The Server Dashboard shows active queries, active merges, part mutations and disk usage, lists the other sessions with Terminate Session on each, and reads its slow query list from system.query_log: the most recent finished queries that took longer than a second.

sections.title: Move data
paragraphs: Load {importFormats} files with Import, and export tables or query results as {exportFormats}. A column with even one value that is not valid UTF-8 shows as hex in the grid; select toValidUTF8(column) to read it as text.

faq.question: How do I change a setting for one query?
faq.answer: Put it in a SETTINGS clause on the query itself, such as SELECT … SETTINGS max_threads = 4. Each statement is its own HTTP request with no session, so a separate SET is gone by the next one.

faq.question: Why does port 9000 not connect?
faq.answer: Port 9000 is ClickHouse’s native TCP port, which TablePro does not use. Connect to the HTTP port, or 8443 for HTTPS on ClickHouse Cloud, and check that the server’s HTTP interface is on: a request to /ping on that port answers Ok.
